*Seeing in frequencies*, part 2 of 4. [Fourier analysis](/aboutme/blog/fourier-analysis-from-first-principles/) → **the discrete Fourier world** → [wavelets](/aboutme/blog/wavelets-from-first-principles/) → [wavelets for images](/aboutme/blog/wavelets-for-images/).

Keep every fourth pixel of the image on the left, and rings appear that were never there.

<figure class="fig">
  <canvas data-figure="moire" data-base="/aboutme/blog/spectral/img/" aria-label="Three panels: an image, the same image keeping only every d-th pixel, and the image blurred first and then subsampled."></canvas>
  <div class="controls">
    <span class="seg"><button type="button" data-mimg="zone" class="on">zone plate</button><button type="button" data-mimg="sunset">Sunset</button><button type="button" data-mimg="portrait">Portrait</button></span>
    <span class="seg"><button type="button" data-d="2">every 2nd</button><button type="button" data-d="3">every 3rd</button><button type="button" data-d="4" class="on">every 4th</button></span>
  </div>
  <div class="insight" data-insight></div>
</figure>

The rings in the middle panel are **aliases**: fine detail that could not survive the subsampling and came back as coarse detail instead. The right panel, blurred before subsampling, has none. This post explains exactly why, and then everything else that changes when the clean integrals of [Part 1](/aboutme/blog/fourier-analysis-from-first-principles/) meet a computer: signals are **sampled**, and they are **finite**.

Almost every bug in spectral code is one of these two facts forgotten. Sampling makes spectra periodic (Section 2), which is aliasing; finiteness makes them leak (Section 7), which is why a pure tone shows up in every bin. Between those two sections the post builds the discrete Fourier transform by hand in one and two dimensions, and then the FFT, the fast algorithm that computes it. It ends with the theorem that limits all of this, the uncertainty principle, and the tool built on it, the spectrogram, which is where wavelets begin.

## Notation and conventions

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $T$, $f_s = 1/T$ | sampling interval and rate |
| $x[n] = f(nT)$ | samples |
| $X(\nu)$ | discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT) |
| $N$ | number of samples |
| $\omega_N = e^{-2\pi i/N}$ | the DFT's root of unity |
| $X[k] = \sum_n x[n]\,\omega_N^{kn}$ | discrete Fourier transform (DFT) |
| $\mathbf{F}$ | the $N \times N$ DFT matrix, $\mathbf{F}_{kn} = \omega_N^{kn}$ |
| $x \circledast y$ | circular convolution |

Frequencies are in cycles per unit (Hz for time, cycles per pixel for images), as in Part 1. The DFT follows NumPy: no factor on the forward transform, $1/N$ on the inverse.

## 1. Four Fourier transforms, one rule

Part 1 met two transforms: the Fourier series (periodic signals) and the Fourier transform (signals on the whole line). Sampling adds two more, and the four sit on a two-by-two grid.

<figure class="sketch-fig">
<svg class="sketch" viewBox="0 0 960 640" role="img" aria-label="A two by two map of the four Fourier transforms. Continuous, non-periodic signals have the Fourier transform, whose spectrum is continuous and not periodic. Continuous periodic signals have Fourier series: a discrete line spectrum. Discrete non-periodic signals have the discrete-time Fourier transform, whose spectrum is continuous and periodic. Discrete periodic signals have the discrete Fourier transform, discrete and periodic in both domains, which is what the FFT computes. The rule: discrete in one domain if and only if periodic in the other."><text x="480" y="40" text-anchor="middle" style="font-family:Kalam,cursive;font-size:26px;font-weight:700;fill:var(--a1)">four | Signal in time | Spectrum | Name |
|---|---|---|
| continuous, not periodic | continuous, not periodic | Fourier transform |
| continuous, periodic | discrete | Fourier series |
| discrete, not periodic | continuous, periodic | DTFT |
| discrete, periodic | discrete, periodic | DFT |

One rule organises the table: **discrete in one domain if and only if periodic in the other**. Part 1 proved half of it already: a periodic signal has a discrete spectrum, the Fourier series. Section 2 proves the other half: a sampled signal has a periodic spectrum. A computer can only hold finitely many numbers in each domain, so it must be discrete in both, hence periodic in both: that is the DFT.

:::question
"The FFT computes the Fourier transform." What does it actually compute?
:::

:::answer
The DFT of $N$ numbers. Read as a statement about a continuous signal, that is the Fourier transform of the signal after three changes: it was sampled (so its spectrum is replaced by the sum of shifted copies, Section 2), cut to $N$ samples (so the spectrum is smeared by a sinc, Section 7), and treated as periodic (so the spectrum is read at only $N$ frequencies, Section 4). Each change has a visible consequence, and each has a fix.
:::

## 2. Sampling

### Poisson summation: sampling one side samples the other

One identity does most of the work in this post. It relates samples of a function to samples of its transform.

:::theorem[Poisson summation]
For a smooth, rapidly decaying $f$,
$$
\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} f(n) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\hat f(k), \qquad \text{and more generally} \qquad \sum_{n} f(nT) = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{k}\hat f\!\left(\frac{k}{T}\right).
$$
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Make a periodic function.** Let $F(x) = \sum_n f(x + n)$. Because $f$ decays fast the sum converges and is smooth, and $F(x + 1) = F(x)$.

**Step 2. Its Fourier coefficients are samples of $\hat f$.** $c_k(F) = \int_0^1\sum_n f(x + n)\,e^{-2\pi ikx}dx = \sum_n\int_n^{n+1}f(u)\,e^{-2\pi ik(u - n)}du$ (substitute $u = x + n$). Since $e^{2\pi ikn} = 1$, this is $\sum_n\int_n^{n+1}f(u)e^{-2\pi iku}du = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(u)e^{-2\pi iku}du = \hat f(k)$: the integrals over the unit intervals tile the line.

**Step 3. Evaluate the series at $0$.** $F$ is smooth, so its coefficients decay fast (Part 1, Section 4) and its Fourier series converges to it at every point. At $x = 0$: $F(0) = \sum_k c_k(F)$, that is, $\sum_n f(n) = \sum_k\hat f(k)$.

**Step 4. Other spacings.** Apply this to $g(x) = f(Tx)$, whose transform is $\hat g(\xi) = \frac1T\hat f(\xi/T)$ by the scaling rule: $\sum_n f(nT) = \frac1T\sum_k\hat f(k/T)$.
:::

### Sampling makes the spectrum periodic

Sample $f$ every $T$: $x[n] = f(nT)$. The natural transform of a sequence is the **discrete-time Fourier transform**, $X(\nu) = \sum_n x[n]\,e^{-2\pi i\nu nT}$, a function of frequency $\nu$ in Hz. It is periodic with period $f_s$, since adding $f_s$ to $\nu$ multiplies each term by $e^{-2\pi i n} = 1$. What is it, in terms of $\hat f$?

:::proposition[The sampled spectrum is a sum of shifted copies]
$$
X(\nu) = f_s\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\hat f(\nu - k f_s).
$$
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Fold the exponential into the function.** Let $g(x) = f(x)e^{-2\pi i\nu x}$. Then $X(\nu) = \sum_n g(nT)$.

**Step 2. Its transform is a shift.** By the modulation rule, $\hat g(\xi) = \hat f(\xi + \nu)$.

**Step 3. Poisson summation** with spacing $T$: $\sum_n g(nT) = \frac1T\sum_k\hat g(k/T) = f_s\sum_k\hat f(\nu + kf_s)$. Relabel $k \to -k$.
:::

Sampling every $T$ seconds places a copy of the spectrum at every multiple of $f_s$. If $f$ contains no frequencies at or above $f_s/2$, the copies sit side by side and the original can be read off the central one. If it does, they overlap, and in the overlap the frequencies of different copies add up and can no longer be separated. That overlap is **aliasing**.

<figure class="fig">
<video autoplay muted loop playsinline controls preload="metadata" poster="/aboutme/blog/spectral/aliasing.jpg"><source src="/aboutme/blog/spectral/aliasing.webm" type="video/webm" /><source src="/aboutme/blog/spectral/aliasing.mp4" type="video/mp4" /></video>
<figcaption>The spectrum of a band-limited signal (teal) and the copies that sampling creates. Above twice the bandwidth they stay apart; below it they overlap (amber), and the overlap is aliasing.</figcaption>
</figure>

### The sampling theorem

:::theorem[Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem]
If $\hat f(\xi) = 0$ for all $\lvert\xi\rvert \ge f_s/2$, then $f$ is determined by its samples, and
$$
f(x) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} f(nT)\,\operatorname{sinc}\!\big(f_s x - n\big).
$$
The frequency $f_s/2$ is the **Nyquist frequency**.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Only one copy is non-zero in the band.** For $\lvert\nu\rvert < f_s/2$, every copy $\hat f(\nu - kf_s)$ with $k \ne 0$ is evaluated at a frequency of size at least $f_s/2$, where $\hat f$ vanishes. So $X(\nu) = f_s\hat f(\nu)$ there.

**Step 2. Invert $\hat f$ over the band.** $f(x) = \int_{-f_s/2}^{f_s/2}\hat f(\nu)e^{2\pi i\nu x}d\nu = \frac{1}{f_s}\int_{-f_s/2}^{f_s/2}X(\nu)e^{2\pi i\nu x}d\nu$.

**Step 3. Insert the samples.** Substitute $X(\nu) = \sum_n f(nT)e^{-2\pi i\nu nT}$ and exchange sum and integral (valid for the nice $f$ we assume): $f(x) = \sum_n f(nT)\cdot\frac1{f_s}\int_{-f_s/2}^{f_s/2}e^{2\pi i\nu(x - nT)}d\nu$.

**Step 4. The integral is a sinc.** $\int_{-f_s/2}^{f_s/2}e^{2\pi i\nu u}d\nu = \frac{\sin(\pi f_s u)}{\pi u} = f_s\operatorname{sinc}(f_s u)$ (the box pair of Part 1 with duality). With $u = x - nT$, $f_s u = f_sx - n$.
:::

Checked numerically: $\operatorname{sinc}^2(6x)$, whose spectrum fills $[-6, 6]$ Hz, sampled at 14 Hz and rebuilt from 801 samples, matches itself to $2\times10^{-10}$.

### What aliasing looks like

A single cosine makes aliasing concrete. Sampled at rate $f_s$, the waves $e^{2\pi i f t}$ and $e^{2\pi i(f + mf_s)t}$ agree at every sample, because $e^{2\pi imf_s\cdot nT} = e^{2\pi imn} = 1$. So a frequency $f$ is indistinguishable from $f - mf_s$ for every whole $m$, and reconstruction picks the one inside $[-f_s/2, f_s/2]$. A 7 Hz wave sampled at 10 Hz produces exactly the samples of a 3 Hz wave (checked to machine precision).

    <label class="slider">sample rate (Hz) <input type="range" min="2" max="24" step="0.5" value="10" data-fs /> <span class="mono" data-fsval>10.0</span></label>
    <label class="slider">phase <input type="range" min="0" max="3.1416" step="0.01" value="0.6" data-ph /> <span class="mono" data-phval>34°</span></label>
  </div>

</figure>

Three things people get wrong about the theorem:

1. **"Sample at twice the frequency."** At exactly $f_s = 2f$ the samples of $\cos(2\pi ft + \varphi)$ are $(-1)^n\cos\varphi$, which vanish for a sine. The theorem needs the signal *strictly* below $f_s/2$. Set the figure to $f = 5$, $f_s = 10$ and move the phase.
2. **"The rate depends on the highest frequency."** It depends on the width of the band. A signal confined to $[f_L, f_H]$ can be sampled at as little as $2(f_H - f_L)$ under conditions on where the band sits (**bandpass sampling**), because the copies can interleave without overlapping. Radio receivers rely on this.
3. **"Subsampling an image is free."** Keeping every $d$-th pixel is sampling at $1/d$ of the rate, so everything above $1/(2d)$ cycles per pixel aliases. That is the opening figure: the zone plate's rings have frequency $r/256$ cycles per pixel at radius $r$, so with $d = 4$ everything beyond radius $32$ folds back. Image libraries blur before shrinking for this reason (`antialias=True` in PyTorch's `interpolate`; PIL's default resampling filters).

## 3. Aliasing inside neural networks

A strided convolution or a pooling layer keeps every other sample. Section 2 says what that does to anything above a quarter of the sampling rate: it folds. A consequence that surprised the deep-learning community is that **convolutional networks are not shift-invariant**: move the input by one pixel and the output of a strided layer changes, often a lot (Azulay and Weiss, 2019). Zhang (2019) applied the textbook fix, blur before subsampling ("BlurPool"), and recovered much of the lost invariance; Karras et al. (2021) built StyleGAN3 around alias-free signal processing to stop textures from sticking to pixel coordinates.

<figure class="fig">
  <canvas data-figure="stride" aria-label="A signal with a slow wave and a texture near the Nyquist frequency, shifted by a slider. Below, the output of plain stride-2 subsampling and of blur-then-stride. Right, the output energy for each of eight shifts."></canvas>
  <div class="controls">
    <label class="slider">shift <input type="range" min="0" max="7" step="1" value="0" data-shift /> <span class="mono" data-shiftval>0</span></label>
  </div>
  <div class="insight" data-insight></div>
</figure>

The input is a slow wave plus a texture at $0.47$ cycles per sample. Plain stride-2 subsampling folds the texture into a slow false wave whose size depends on where the samples land: over eight one-sample shifts the output energy varies by 19% (standard deviation over mean). Blurring with $[1, 2, 1]/4$ first, whose frequency response is $\cos^2(\pi\xi)$, passes the slow wave ($0.98$) and almost erases the texture ($0.009$): variation 0%. The price is lost detail; the network must decide what it was going to throw away anyway.

## 4. The DFT, by hand

Now finiteness. Take $N$ samples $x[0], \ldots, x[N-1]$. Their DTFT, in cycles per sample, is $X(\nu) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-2\pi i\nu n}$, a continuous, 1-periodic function. A computer stores finitely many of its values, and the natural choice is $N$ equally spaced ones.

:::definition[Discrete Fourier transform]
$$
X[k] = X\!\left(\frac kN\right) = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]\,e^{-2\pi ikn/N} = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]\,\omega_N^{kn}, \qquad k = 0, \ldots, N - 1 .
$$
In matrix form $\boldsymbol{X} = \mathbf{F}\boldsymbol{x}$ with $\mathbf{F}_{kn} = \omega_N^{kn}$, $\omega_N = e^{-2\pi i/N}$.
:::

:::proposition[The DFT is invertible, and unitary up to scale]
$\mathbf{F}^{\mathsf H}\mathbf{F} = N\mathbf{I}$. Hence $x[n] = \frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X[k]\,e^{2\pi ikn/N}$, and $\sum_k\lvert X[k]\rvert^2 = N\sum_n\lvert x[n]\rvert^2$ (Parseval).
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. An entry of $\mathbf{F}^{\mathsf H}\mathbf{F}$.** $(\mathbf{F}^{\mathsf H}\mathbf{F})_{nm} = \sum_k\overline{\omega_N^{kn}}\,\omega_N^{km} = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ik(n - m)/N}$.

**Step 2. A geometric sum.** With $r = e^{2\pi i(n - m)/N}$: if $n = m$ every term is $1$ and the sum is $N$. If $n \ne m$ (both in $0..N-1$), then $r \ne 1$ and the sum is $\frac{1 - r^N}{1 - r} = 0$, because $r^N = e^{2\pi i(n - m)} = 1$.

**Step 3. Consequences.** $\mathbf{F}^{-1} = \frac1N\mathbf{F}^{\mathsf H}$ gives the inverse formula, and $\lVert\boldsymbol{X}\rVert^2 = \boldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf H}\mathbf{F}^{\mathsf H}\mathbf{F}\boldsymbol{x} = N\lVert\boldsymbol{x}\rVert^2$. (Some libraries divide both directions by $\sqrt N$ to make $\mathbf{F}$ exactly unitary; NumPy's `norm="ortho"`.)
:::

The inverse formula defines $x[n]$ for *every* integer $n$, and the values repeat with period $N$. So the DFT silently treats your $N$ samples as one period of a periodic signal: the bottom-right corner of the map in Section 1.

:::example[A 4-point DFT by hand]
With $N = 4$, $\omega_4 = e^{-i\pi/2} = -i$, so every entry of $\mathbf{F}$ is one of $1, -i, -1, i$:
$$
\mathbf{F} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & -i & -1 & i\\ 1 & -1 & 1 & -1\\ 1 & i & -1 & -i\end{bmatrix}.
$$
For $\boldsymbol{x} = (1, 2, 0, -1)$:
- $X[0] = 1 + 2 + 0 - 1 = 2$ (the sum: the DC term);
- $X[1] = 1 + 2(-i) + 0(-1) + (-1)(i) = 1 - 3i$;
- $X[2] = 1 - 2 + 0 + 1 = 0$;
- $X[3] = 1 + 2i + 0 + (-1)(-i) = 1 + 3i$.

$X[3] = \overline{X[1]}$, as it must for real input (Part 1, Section 3): index $3$ is frequency $-1$. NumPy agrees: `np.fft.fft([1, 2, 0, -1])` gives `[2, 1-3j, 0, 1+3j]`.
:::

:::example[An 8-point box]
$\boldsymbol{x} = (1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0)$. Then $X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{3}\omega_8^{kn} = \frac{1 - \omega_8^{4k}}{1 - \omega_8^k}$ for $k \ne 0$, and $\omega_8^{4k} = (-1)^k$. So $X[0] = 4$, $X[k] = 0$ for even $k \ne 0$, and $X[k] = \frac{2}{1 - \omega_8^k}$ for odd $k$: numerically $X[1] = 1 - 2.414i$, $X[3] = 1 - 0.414i$, and their conjugates at $k = 7, 5$. This is a sampled sinc, the discrete cousin of Part 1's box pair. Section 8 computes it again, fast.
:::

### Circular convolution

:::proposition[The DFT turns circular convolution into multiplication]
With $(x\circledast y)[n] = \sum_{m=0}^{N-1}x[m]\,y[(n - m)\bmod N]$, the DFT of $x\circledast y$ is $X[k]\,Y[k]$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Write it out.** $\sum_n\sum_m x[m]\,y[(n - m)\bmod N]\,\omega_N^{kn}$.

**Step 2. Split the exponent** as $\omega_N^{kn} = \omega_N^{km}\omega_N^{k(n - m)}$ and swap the sums: $\sum_m x[m]\omega_N^{km}\sum_n y[(n - m)\bmod N]\,\omega_N^{k(n-m)}$.

**Step 3. The inner sum is $Y[k]$.** As $n$ runs over $0..N-1$, $j = (n - m)\bmod N$ also runs over $0..N-1$, and $\omega_N^{k(n - m)} = \omega_N^{kj}$ because $\omega_N^N = 1$. What remains is $X[k]Y[k]$.
:::

The "mod $N$" is the catch. Multiplying two DFTs computes a convolution that **wraps around**. Convolve $(1, 2, 3)$ with $(1, 1)$: the true result is $(1, 3, 5, 3)$, but with $N = 3$ the last value wraps onto the first and you get $(4, 3, 5)$. The fix is to zero-pad both signals to length at least $L + M - 1$ for lengths $L$ and $M$: with $N = 4$ the product of DFTs returns $(1, 3, 5, 3)$ exactly.

## 5. The 2-D DFT, by hand

Images are where the 2-D DFT lives, and courses usually skip from the formula to the picture. Small cases can be done by hand.

:::definition[2-D DFT]
For an $M \times N$ image $x[m, n]$ (row $m$, column $n$),
$$
X[k, l] = \sum_{m=0}^{M-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[m, n]\,\omega_M^{km}\,\omega_N^{ln}.
$$
:::

:::proposition[Rows, then columns]
The 2-D DFT is a 1-D DFT of every row followed by a 1-D DFT of every column (or the other way round).
:::

:::proof
Group the sum: $X[k, l] = \sum_m\omega_M^{km}\Big(\sum_n x[m, n]\,\omega_N^{ln}\Big)$. The bracket, for each row $m$, is the 1-D DFT of that row at frequency $l$; the outer sum is a 1-D DFT down each column of the result. Because the sums are finite, they can be taken in either order.
:::

:::example[Two images by hand]
**A $2 \times 2$ image** $\begin{bmatrix}a & b\\ c & d\end{bmatrix}$. With $N = 2$, $\omega_2 = -1$, so every factor is $\pm1$:
$$
X = \begin{bmatrix}a + b + c + d & a - b + c - d\\ a + b - c - d & a - b - c + d\end{bmatrix}.
$$
Sum, left minus right, top minus bottom, checker. Remember these four; [Part 4](/aboutme/blog/wavelets-for-images/) shows that, divided by 4, they are exactly one level of the 2-D Haar wavelet transform.

**A $4 \times 4$ image of vertical stripes**, $x[m, n] = 1$ when $n$ is even. The image does not depend on $m$, so the column sum is $\sum_m(-i)^{km} = 4$ if $k = 0$ and $0$ otherwise. Along a row, $\sum_{n\in\{0,2\}}(-i)^{ln} = 1 + (-1)^l$, which is $2$ for even $l$ and $0$ for odd $l$. So exactly two coefficients survive: $X[0, 0] = 8$ (the mean, times 16) and $X[0, 2] = 8$ (the stripes: two cycles across each row).
:::

Check these, and any other $4 \times 4$ pattern, below. Click pixels to change the image, click a coefficient to see the factor $1$, $-i$, $-1$ or $i$ that each pixel is multiplied by.

<figure class="fig">
  <canvas data-figure="dft4" aria-label="Three 4 by 4 grids: an image of zeros and ones, its 2-D DFT, and for one chosen coefficient the factor (1, minus i, minus 1 or i) that multiplies each pixel."></canvas>
  <div class="controls">
    <span class="seg"><button type="button" data-p4="vstripes" class="on">vertical stripes</button><button type="button" data-p4="hstripes">horizontal stripes</button><button type="button" data-p4="checker">checkerboard</button><button type="button" data-p4="pixel">one pixel</button><button type="button" data-p4="block">2 × 2 block</button><button type="button" data-p4="constant">constant</button></span>
  </div>
  <div class="insight" data-insight></div>
</figure>

:::question
Which index is the "horizontal frequency"?
:::

:::answer
In NumPy's `fft2(x)`, axis 0 is rows, so the first index $k$ counts cycles going **down** the image (vertical frequency) and $l$ counts cycles going **across** (horizontal frequency). Vertical stripes therefore live at $(0, l)$. Because image rows run downward, a spectrum displayed as an image is upside down relative to a mathematics textbook's $(\xi, \eta)$ plane, where $\eta$ points up. Neither is wrong; say which you use.
:::

style="font-family:Kalam,cursive;font-size:16px;font-weight:400;fill:var(--muted)">bin spacing fs / N = 1 Hz;  real input: X[N − k] = conj X[k], so the right half repeats the left</text><text x="450" y="380" text-anchor="middle" style="font-family:Kalam,cursive;font-size:16px;font-weight:400;fill:var(--muted)">rfft keeps k = 0 … N/2: N/2 + 1 numbers</text></svg>
</figure>

- **Bin $k$ is frequency $k f_s/N$** for $k < N/2$, and $(k - N)f_s/N$ for $k > N/2$: the upper half holds the negative frequencies, because the DFT is periodic in $k$ with period $N$.
- **Bin $N/2$** (for even $N$) is the Nyquist frequency, shared by $+f_s/2$ and $-f_s/2$; for real input it is real.
- **`fftfreq(N, d=T)`** returns these frequencies; **`fftshift`** reorders the output so zero is in the middle (in 2-D, both axes).
- **Real input** gives $X[N - k] = \overline{X[k]}$, so half the output is redundant. **`rfft`** returns only $k = 0, \ldots, N/2$, which is $N/2 + 1$ numbers; `rfft2` on an $M \times N$ image returns $M \times (N/2 + 1)$.
- **Resolution** is $f_s/N$: one over the *duration* of the record. More samples per second raise the Nyquist frequency; a longer record sharpens the frequency spacing.

## 7. Leakage and windows

Ask an FFT for the spectrum of a pure tone and it usually answers with every bin.

:::proposition[A tone between bins leaks into all of them]
For $x[n] = e^{2\pi if_0n/N}$, $n = 0, \ldots, N-1$, with $f_0$ in cycles per record,
$$
\lvert X[k]\rvert = \left\lvert\frac{\sin\big(\pi(f_0 - k)\big)}{\sin\big(\pi(f_0 - k)/N\big)}\right\rvert .
$$
If $f_0$ is a whole number this is $N$ at $k = f_0$ and $0$ elsewhere. Otherwise it is non-zero at every $k$, and falls off only like $1/\lvert f_0 - k\rvert$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. A geometric sum.** $X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi i(f_0 - k)n/N} = \frac{1 - e^{2\pi i(f_0 - k)}}{1 - e^{2\pi i(f_0 - k)/N}}$ when the ratio is not $1$.

**Step 2. Factor half-angles.** $1 - e^{2i\theta} = -2i\,e^{i\theta}\sin\theta$. Applied to the numerator ($\theta = \pi(f_0 - k)$) and the denominator ($\theta = \pi(f_0 - k)/N$), the magnitudes of the phase factors are $1$, leaving the ratio of sines.

**Step 3. Whole $f_0$.** The numerator $\sin(\pi(f_0 - k))$ vanishes for every integer $k$; at $k = f_0$ the sum is simply $N$ terms equal to $1$.

**Step 4. Decay.** For $\lvert f_0 - k\rvert \ll N$, $\sin(\pi(f_0 - k)/N) \approx \pi(f_0 - k)/N$, so $\lvert X[k]\rvert \approx N\lvert\sin\pi(f_0 - k)\rvert/(\pi\lvert f_0 - k\rvert)$.
:::

Why? The DFT pretends the record repeats. A tone that does not fit a whole number of cycles into the record has a **jump** where the end meets the start, and Part 1 showed what a jump costs: slowly decaying coefficients. Two numbers measured on $N = 64$: a cosine exactly on bin 10 lights 2 bins (bins 10 and 54, the negative frequency); a cosine at bin 10.5 lights all 64, and its peak drops to $0.65$ of its true height ($-3.8$ dB, the "scalloping loss").

**Windows** taper the record to zero at both ends, removing the jump. The Hann window, $w[n] = \tfrac12 - \tfrac12\cos(2\pi n/N)$, is the clearest case: since $\cos(2\pi n/N) = \tfrac12(e^{2\pi in/N} + e^{-2\pi in/N})$ and multiplying by $e^{\pm2\pi in/N}$ shifts a DFT by one bin, a windowed spectrum is $\tfrac12X[k] - \tfrac14X[k - 1] - \tfrac14X[k + 1]$. The leakage of neighbouring bins has alternating signs, and this combination cancels most of it. The cost is a wider main lobe. Measured on 64 samples with heavy zero-padding:

| Window | Main lobe half-width | Highest side lobe |
|---|---|---|
| none (rectangular) | 1 bin | −13.3 dB |
| Hann | 2 bins | −31.5 dB |
| Blackman | 3 bins | −58.1 dB |

:::question
Zero-padding a signal before the FFT gives more frequency bins. Does it give more resolution?
:::

:::answer
No. Padding $N$ samples with zeros to length $PN$ returns the same DTFT $X(\nu)$ sampled $P$ times more densely: a smoother drawing of the same curve. What decides whether two tones can be told apart is the curve itself, whose main lobes are about $1/N$ wide. Measured: two tones $0.7$ bins apart in 64 samples (Hann window) show one peak with padding $\times1$, $\times4$ and $\times16$, and two peaks when the record is four times longer. Padding is useful for locating a single peak precisely and for avoiding wrap-around in convolution, not for resolution.
:::

### The bright cross in image spectra

The same mechanism explains the bright "+" through the centre of many image spectra. The 2-D DFT treats the image as a tile of a periodic wallpaper, so wherever the left edge differs from the right (or the top from the bottom) there is a jump along a whole border, and its slowly decaying energy lands on the axes. The standard remedy is to remove the jump without touching the image's content: Moisan's **periodic plus smooth decomposition** writes $u = p + s$, where $s$ is the smooth function (solving a discrete Laplace equation) that carries the border mismatch, and $p$ is periodic. In the DFT, $\hat s[q, r] = \hat v[q, r]/\big(2\cos\frac{2\pi q}{M} + 2\cos\frac{2\pi r}{N} - 4\big)$, where $v$ is zero except along the four borders, where it holds the difference between opposite edges.

![The Eye sketch, its log spectrum with a bright cross along the axes, and the log spectrum of its periodic component, where the cross is much weaker.](/aboutme/blog/spectral/cross_eye.png)

But the cross is not always an artefact. Measuring the average power on the axes against the average power off them, at the same radii (16 to 120 cycles per image): for the *Eye*, whose borders differ, removing the border jump lowers the excess from 6.2× to 3.6×. For the *Portrait* it stays at 3.1×, because there the cross comes from genuine horizontal and vertical structure. Do not assume; decompose and compare.

## 8. The FFT

Computed directly, the DFT costs $N^2$ multiplications. The fast Fourier transform computes exactly the same numbers with about $\frac N2\log_2N$, by noticing that a DFT of even length is two DFTs of half the length.

:::proposition[Radix-2 decimation in time]
Let $N$ be even, and let $E[k]$ and $O[k]$ be the $N/2$-point DFTs of the even-indexed and odd-indexed samples. Then for $k = 0, \ldots, N/2 - 1$,
$$
X[k] = E[k] + \omega_N^k\,O[k], \qquad X[k + N/2] = E[k] - \omega_N^k\,O[k].
$$
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Split the sum** by parity of $n$: $X[k] = \sum_{m=0}^{N/2-1}x[2m]\,\omega_N^{2mk} + \sum_{m=0}^{N/2-1}x[2m+1]\,\omega_N^{(2m+1)k}$.

**Step 2. Halve the root of unity.** $\omega_N^2 = e^{-4\pi i/N} = \omega_{N/2}$. So the first sum is $\sum_m x[2m]\,\omega_{N/2}^{mk} = E[k]$ and the second is $\omega_N^k\sum_m x[2m+1]\,\omega_{N/2}^{mk} = \omega_N^kO[k]$.

**Step 3. The other half.** $E$ and $O$ are periodic with period $N/2$, and $\omega_N^{k + N/2} = \omega_N^ke^{-i\pi} = -\omega_N^k$. Substituting $k + N/2$ gives $E[k] - \omega_N^kO[k]$.
:::

:::proposition[Cost]
If $N$ is a power of two, applying the split recursively uses $C(N) = \frac N2\log_2 N$ complex multiplications.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Recurrence.** One level does two half-size transforms and $N/2$ multiplications by $\omega_N^k$ (each product $\omega_N^kO[k]$ is used twice): $C(N) = 2C(N/2) + N/2$, with $C(1) = 0$.

**Step 2. Induction.** If $C(N/2) = \frac N4\log_2\frac N2$, then $C(N) = \frac N2(\log_2N - 1) + \frac N2 = \frac N2\log_2N$.
:::

For $N = 2^{20}$, about a million samples, that is about ten million multiplications instead of a trillion.

:::example[The 8-point box, through the butterflies]
Even samples $(1, 1, 0, 0)$, odd samples $(1, 1, 0, 0)$: the same, so $E = O = (2,\ 1 - i,\ 0,\ 1 + i)$ (a 4-point DFT, by the rule of Section 4). Then $X[1] = E[1] + \omega_8\,O[1] = (1 - i)(1 + \omega_8)$ with $\omega_8 = \frac{1 - i}{\sqrt2}$: $(1 - i) + \frac{(1 - i)^2}{\sqrt2} = 1 - i - \sqrt2\,i = 1 - 2.414i$, matching Section 4. And $X[5] = E[1] - \omega_8O[1] = 1 - i + \sqrt2\,i = 1 + 0.414i$.
:::

:::question
Is the FFT a different transform from the DFT?
:::

:::answer
No. It is an algorithm that computes the DFT exactly (up to round-off, which grows only like $\log N$). Any difference between `fft(x)` and a direct $N^2$ sum is floating-point error.
:::

**How real libraries do it.** Production FFTs (FFTW, pocketfft inside NumPy and SciPy, cuFFT on GPUs) are not limited to powers of two. Mixed-radix algorithms split $N$ into any factors, and Bluestein's algorithm turns a prime length into a convolution of power-of-two length, so every $N$ costs $O(N\log N)$; but the constant depends on $N$'s factors. Measured with SciPy on my laptop: length $65{,}536 = 2^{16}$ took 0.55 ms, the prime $65{,}537$ took 2.11 ms, and $65{,}610 = 2\cdot3^8\cdot5$ (what `scipy.fft.next_fast_len(65537)` suggests) took 0.40 ms. Pad to a fast length when you can. FFT convolution beats direct convolution once the kernel is long enough: convolving 16,384 samples, the crossover on the same laptop fell between kernel lengths 64 and 128 (direct 0.15 ms vs FFT 0.18 ms at 64; 0.24 vs 0.17 ms at 128). CNN kernels are tiny, which is why deep-learning libraries mostly convolve directly.

## 9. The DCT, and why JPEG uses it

Section 7 showed that the DFT's hidden periodic extension creates jumps at the borders. There is a cleaner way to make a finite signal periodic: reflect it. The mirrored sequence $x[0], \ldots, x[N-1], x[N-1], \ldots, x[0]$ has no jump anywhere, only kinks, and by Part 1 its coefficients decay like $1/k^2$ instead of $1/k$.

:::proposition[The DCT is the DFT of the mirrored signal]
Let $y$ be the length-$2N$ mirror extension of $x$. Then its DFT is $Y[k] = 2e^{i\pi k/(2N)}\,C[k]$ with the **DCT-II**
$$
C[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]\cos\!\Big(\frac{\pi k(n + \tfrac12)}{N}\Big).
$$
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Pair each sample with its mirror image.** $y[n] = y[2N - 1 - n] = x[n]$ for $n < N$, so $Y[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]\big(e^{-2\pi ikn/(2N)} + e^{-2\pi ik(2N - 1 - n)/(2N)}\big)$.

**Step 2. Simplify the second exponential.** $e^{-2\pi ik(2N - 1 - n)/(2N)} = e^{-2\pi ik}\,e^{i\pi k(n + 1)/N} = e^{i\pi k(n+1)/N}$.

**Step 3. Factor out half a step.** $e^{-i\pi kn/N} + e^{i\pi k(n+1)/N} = e^{i\pi k/(2N)}\big(e^{-i\pi k(n + 1/2)/N} + e^{i\pi k(n + 1/2)/N}\big) = 2e^{i\pi k/(2N)}\cos\big(\pi k(n + \tfrac12)/N\big)$.
:::

Measured on a ramp of 64 samples (the worst case for the DFT, since its two ends differ by the full range): coefficient size falls by a factor of about 2.3 to 2.9 each time $k$ triples for the DFT, roughly $1/k$, and by about 9 for the DCT, roughly $1/k^2$. The first four DCT coefficients hold 99.8% of the (mean-removed) energy; the first four DFT frequencies hold 86.8%. **Energy compaction** is the whole point of a compression transform: few large coefficients, many negligible ones.

JPEG applies the 2-D DCT to each $8\times8$ block, divides each coefficient by an entry of a quantisation table (large for high frequencies) and rounds. At low quality most high-frequency coefficients round to zero, and since each block is coded alone, the blocks stop agreeing at their borders.

![A 64 by 64 crop of the Eye sketch: the original, and the same crop after JPEG compression at quality 8, where 8 by 8 blocks are clearly visible.](/aboutme/blog/spectral/jpeg_blocks.png)

At quality 8 the whole $256\times256$ sketch compresses from 65,536 bytes to 1,939, with a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 28.1 dB, and the blocks are plain to see. JPEG 2000 replaced the blocks with a wavelet transform, which is one of the stories of [Part 4](/aboutme/blog/wavelets-for-images/).

## 10. The uncertainty principle

Part 1 showed that squeezing a function widens its transform. How far can both be narrow at once? Measure the spread of $\lvert f\rvert^2$ and of $\lvert\hat f\rvert^2$ by their standard deviations.

:::theorem[Heisenberg–Gabor uncertainty principle]
Let $f$ be smooth and decaying with $\int\lvert f\rvert^2 = 1$, and let
$\sigma_x^2 = \int(x - \bar x)^2\lvert f(x)\rvert^2dx$, $\sigma_\xi^2 = \int(\xi - \bar\xi)^2\lvert\hat f(\xi)\rvert^2d\xi$, where $\bar x$, $\bar\xi$ are the means. Then
$$
\sigma_x\,\sigma_\xi \;\ge\; \frac{1}{4\pi},
$$
with equality exactly for Gaussians $f(x) = Ae^{-a(x - \bar x)^2 + 2\pi i\bar\xi x}$, $a > 0$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Centre both.** Replacing $f(x)$ by $e^{-2\pi i\bar\xi x}f(x + \bar x)$ changes neither spread (shift and modulation only move $\lvert f\rvert^2$ and $\lvert\hat f\rvert^2$), so assume $\bar x = \bar\xi = 0$.

**Step 2. Integrate $1$ by parts.** $1 = \int\lvert f\rvert^2dx = \big[x\lvert f\rvert^2\big]_{-\infty}^{\infty} - \int x\,(\lvert f\rvert^2)'dx = -\int x\,(\lvert f\rvert^2)'dx$; the boundary term vanishes because $f$ decays.

**Step 3. Differentiate $\lvert f\rvert^2 = f\overline f$.** $(f\overline f)' = f'\overline f + f\overline{f'} = 2\operatorname{Re}(\overline f f')$. So $1 = -2\operatorname{Re}\int x\overline f f'dx \le 2\int\lvert xf\rvert\,\lvert f'\rvert\,dx$.

**Step 4. Cauchy–Schwarz.** $\int\lvert xf\rvert\lvert f'\rvert \le \big(\int x^2\lvert f\rvert^2\big)^{1/2}\big(\int\lvert f'\rvert^2\big)^{1/2} = \sigma_x\lVert f'\rVert$.

**Step 5. Plancherel and the derivative rule.** $\lVert f'\rVert^2 = \int\lvert2\pi i\xi\hat f(\xi)\rvert^2d\xi = 4\pi^2\sigma_\xi^2$, so $\lVert f'\rVert = 2\pi\sigma_\xi$.

**Step 6. Combine.** $1 \le 2\sigma_x\cdot2\pi\sigma_\xi$.

**Step 7. Equality.** Cauchy–Schwarz is tight only when $f' = c\,xf$ for a constant $c$, and Step 3 is tight only when $c$ is real and negative. Solving $f' = cxf$ gives $f = Ae^{cx^2/2}$, a Gaussian.
:::

Measured: a Gaussian gives $\sigma_x\sigma_\xi = 0.07958 = 1/(4\pi)$ to five digits; $e^{-\lvert x\rvert}$ gives $0.1125$ and $\operatorname{sech}x$ gives $0.0833$, both above the bound.

:::question
Is this about measurement, as in quantum mechanics?
:::

:::answer
No. It is a theorem about a function and its Fourier transform, true before anyone measures anything. Quantum mechanics inherits it because a particle's position and momentum wavefunctions are a Fourier pair. In signal processing it says something equally concrete: a pulse lasting $1$ ms (as a standard deviation) cannot have a frequency spread below $1/(4\pi\cdot0.001) \approx 80$ Hz, whatever the hardware.
:::

The discrete world has its own version, with an elementary proof.

:::theorem[Discrete uncertainty principle (Donoho and Stark, 1989)]
If $\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{C}^N$ is non-zero with $N_t$ non-zero entries and its DFT has $N_\nu$ non-zero entries, then $N_tN_\nu \ge N$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Bound one sample.** By the inverse DFT and the triangle inequality, $\lvert x[n]\rvert \le \frac1N\sum_k\lvert X[k]\rvert$, a sum over the $N_\nu$ non-zero $X[k]$.

**Step 2. Cauchy–Schwarz on that sum.** $\sum_k\lvert X[k]\rvert \le \sqrt{N_\nu}\lVert\boldsymbol{X}\rVert = \sqrt{N_\nu}\sqrt N\lVert\boldsymbol{x}\rVert$, using Parseval from Section 4.

**Step 3. So every sample is small:** $\lvert x[n]\rvert^2 \le \frac{N_\nu}{N}\lVert\boldsymbol{x}\rVert^2$.

**Step 4. Sum over the $N_t$ non-zero samples.** $\lVert\boldsymbol{x}\rVert^2 \le N_t\frac{N_\nu}{N}\lVert\boldsymbol{x}\rVert^2$; divide by $\lVert\boldsymbol{x}\rVert^2 > 0$.
:::

Equality holds for a comb: in $N = 16$, a spike every 4 samples has 4 non-zero entries, and its DFT is again a comb with 4 (checked).

## 11. The short-time Fourier transform

Part 1 ended with a spectrum that knows *what* but not *when*. The obvious fix is to look through a window: multiply by a window $w$ centred at time $\tau$, take the Fourier transform, and slide.

:::definition[Short-time Fourier transform and spectrogram]
$$
S(\tau, \xi) = \int f(t)\,w(t - \tau)\,e^{-2\pi i\xi t}\,dt .
$$
The **spectrogram** is $\lvert S(\tau, \xi)\rvert^2$.
:::

:::proposition[Inversion]
If $w$ is real with $\int w^2 = 1$, then $f(t) = \iint S(\tau, \xi)\,w(t - \tau)\,e^{2\pi i\xi t}\,d\xi\,d\tau$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1.** For fixed $\tau$, $S(\tau, \cdot)$ is the Fourier transform of $g_\tau(t) = f(t)w(t - \tau)$, so by inversion $\int S(\tau, \xi)e^{2\pi i\xi t}d\xi = f(t)w(t - \tau)$.

**Step 2.** Multiply by $w(t - \tau)$ and integrate over $\tau$: $f(t)\int w(t - \tau)^2d\tau = f(t)$.
:::

(The discrete version is "overlap-add": windows that sum to a constant when shifted by the hop, such as Hann at half-overlap, rebuild the signal exactly.)

<figure class="fig">
  <canvas data-figure="spectrogram" aria-label="Spectrogram of the song, frequency from 0 to 300 hertz against time from 0 to 1 second, for a chosen window length."></canvas>
  <div class="controls">
    <span class="seg"><button type="button" data-wl="32">32</button><button type="button" data-wl="64">64</button><button type="button" data-wl="128" class="on">128</button><button type="button" data-wl="256">256</button><button type="button" data-wl="512">512</button></span>
    <span class="mono" style="font-size:0.82rem">window (samples, at 2048 per second)</span>
  </div>
  <div class="insight" data-insight></div>
</figure>

This is the song of Part 1: a chord of two tones 16 Hz apart, a rising chirp, and a click. A window of $L$ samples sees about $L/f_s$ seconds and separates frequencies about $f_s/L$ apart, and the product of the two is fixed. Measured with a peak count on the chord's spectrum: windows of 32, 64 and 128 samples merge the two tones, 256 and 512 resolve them, and the longer the window, the more the click smears. This is the uncertainty principle at work, and no window escapes it. The tiles below show how three transforms divide the time–frequency plane.

<figure class="fig">
<video autoplay muted loop playsinline controls preload="metadata" poster="/aboutme/blog/spectral/tilings.jpg"><source src="/aboutme/blog/spectral/tilings.webm" type="video/webm" /><source src="/aboutme/blog/spectral/tilings.mp4" type="video/mp4" /></video>
<figcaption>Fourier analysis knows frequency exactly and time not at all. The short-time Fourier transform uses one tile shape for every frequency. Wavelets change the shape with frequency: short in time where frequencies are high, long where they are low.</figcaption>
</figure>

A chord wants a long window; a click wants a short one; a chirp wants something in between that changes as it rises. One window for all frequencies is the STFT's limit. Gabor (1946) chose the Gaussian window, which meets the uncertainty bound with equality, but even the best single window is a compromise. The obvious next step, letting the window shrink as the frequency grows, is the wavelet transform of [Part 3](/aboutme/blog/wavelets-from-first-principles/).

## 12. Implementation and caveats

Each trap as symptom, cause and fix:

- **False patterns after resizing.** Aliasing. Low-pass before subsampling (`antialias=True`; a Gaussian with σ ≈ d/2 for a factor d).
- **A pure tone appears in every bin.** Leakage: the record is not a whole number of cycles. Use a window (Hann, Blackman) and accept the wider main lobe.
- **A weak tone is invisible next to a strong one.** The rectangular window's side lobes (−13 dB). Use a low-side-lobe window (Blackman, −58 dB; Blackman–Harris, about −92 dB).
- **Two close tones merge.** The record is too short. Record longer; zero-padding does not help.
- **The start of a convolution is wrong.** Circular wrap-around. Pad to $L + M - 1$.
- **A bright cross in an image spectrum.** Border jumps, or real structure. Use the periodic + smooth decomposition, then compare.
- **An FFT that is oddly slow.** An awkward length (a prime, say). Pad to `scipy.fft.next_fast_len(n)`.
- **Twice the time and memory on real data.** A complex FFT of real input. Use `rfft`, `rfft2`.
- **Features that change when the input moves by a pixel.** Strided layers alias. Blur before the stride (BlurPool), or design alias-free.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import fft, signal

fs, N = 1000.0, 1000
t = np.arange(N) / fs
x = np.cos(2 * np.pi * 50.5 * t) + 1e-3 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * 80 * t)   # a weak tone 60 dB down
X_rect = np.abs(fft.rfft(x))                                        # no window: leakage buries the weak tone
X_bh = np.abs(fft.rfft(x * signal.windows.blackmanharris(N)))      # side lobes near -92 dB: it shows
f = fft.rfftfreq(N, d=1 / fs)                                       # bin frequencies, 1 Hz apart
# measured at 80 Hz: no window, 1.3 dB *below* the neighbouring leakage; Blackman-Harris, 14 dB above it
```

## 13. Where it is used, and what is open

| Use the discrete Fourier toolkit when | Be careful when |
|---|---|
| filtering or convolving long signals, images or volumes | the signal is not periodic and you have not windowed or mirrored |
| measuring periodicities, vibrations, spectra | the record is short relative to the frequencies you need to separate |
| resampling, after a proper low-pass | you subsample without one |
| compressing smooth data (DCT) | the data has many edges (blocks; Part 4 does better) |

**In current work.** Anti-aliased and alias-free networks (BlurPool, StyleGAN3, alias-free U-Nets and neural operators); FFT-based global filtering and long convolutions in vision and sequence models; spectrograms and learned filterbanks as inputs to audio models; compressed sensing and accelerated MRI, which sample *below* the Nyquist rate and recover the rest from a prior; non-uniform FFTs for radio astronomy, MRI with spiral trajectories, and point-cloud learning.

**Open questions.**
1. **Alias-free at low cost.** Exact shift-equivariance needs ideal low-pass filters, and every nonlinearity creates new high frequencies that must be filtered again (Karras et al., 2021). What is the cheapest architecture with a provable bound on aliasing?
2. **Sampling below Nyquist with learned priors.** Compressed sensing has sharp guarantees for sparse signals (Candès, Romberg and Tao, 2006); with generative priors (Bora et al., 2017) the guarantees are partial. When do they hold, and how should failure be detected?
3. **Irregular samples.** Point clouds, sensor networks and unstructured meshes are not on grids. Fast, accurate and differentiable transforms exist (the non-uniform FFT), but how best to build learning layers on them is unsettled.
4. **Learned versus fixed front ends.** Learnable filterbanks sometimes beat fixed spectrograms and sometimes do not. Which properties of a fixed transform (stability, invertibility, the uncertainty trade-off) should a learned one be forced to keep?

:::note[Shoulders to stand on]
- **Brad Osgood, [*Lecture Notes for EE 261: The Fourier Transform and its Applications*](https://see.stanford.edu/Course/EE261)** (Stanford). Sampling, the Dirac comb and Poisson summation, done carefully and kindly.
- **Antonio Torralba, Phillip Isola, William Freeman, [*Foundations of Computer Vision*](https://visionbook.mit.edu/)**, ch. 20–21 (MIT Press, 2024). Sampling, aliasing and resizing, taught on images.
:::

## Self-check

:::question
A 60 Hz mains hum is recorded at 100 samples per second. At what frequency does it appear?
:::

:::answer
$60 - 100 = -40$: it appears at 40 Hz (Section 2), a frequency nobody played.
:::

:::question
You convolve a signal of length 1000 with a filter of length 100 using FFTs. What is the smallest transform length that gives the linear convolution, and what would you actually use?
:::

:::answer
At least $1000 + 100 - 1 = 1099$, or the result wraps around (Section 4). In practice a fast length at or above it: `scipy.fft.next_fast_len(1099)` returns 1100.
:::

:::question
You zero-pad 64 samples to 1024 before the FFT. What improves, and what does not?
:::

:::answer
The spectrum is drawn on a 16 times finer grid, so a single peak can be located more precisely and the plot looks smooth. The ability to separate two close frequencies does not change; it is set by the 64-sample record (Section 7).
:::

:::question
Prove that the DFT of a real signal satisfies $X[N - k] = \overline{X[k]}$.
:::

:::answer
$X[N - k] = \sum_nx[n]\,\omega_N^{(N - k)n} = \sum_nx[n]\,\omega_N^{-kn}$ because $\omega_N^{Nn} = 1$. Since $x[n]$ is real and $\omega_N^{-kn} = \overline{\omega_N^{kn}}$, this is $\overline{\sum_nx[n]\omega_N^{kn}} = \overline{X[k]}$.
:::

:::question
A Gaussian pulse has a time spread $\sigma_t = 1$ ms. What is the smallest possible frequency spread, and which pulses reach it?
:::

:::answer
$\sigma_\xi \ge 1/(4\pi\sigma_t) \approx 80$ Hz; only Gaussians (possibly shifted and modulated) reach it (Section 10).
:::

:::question
Why does a JPEG at low quality show blocks, and why can the DCT not be blamed?
:::

:::answer
The DCT is invertible: on its own it loses nothing. The loss is in rounding the coefficients, which JPEG does independently in every $8\times8$ block, so neighbouring blocks no longer agree along their shared edges (Section 9).
:::
